main_theorem.name: Theorem_10_tensor_regret
main_theorem.statement_math: Theorem 10. Assume that for all $i\in[k]$ and $t=1,\ldots,T$ it holds that $rank(mat_i(G_t))\le r_i$, and let $r=(\prod_{i=1}^k r_i)^{1/k}$. Then the regret of Algorithm 2 compared to any $W^*\in\mathbb{R}^{n_1\times\cdots\times n_k}$ is\n\[\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(W_t)-\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(W^*)\le \sqrt{2r}D\prod_{i=1}^k Tr((H_T^i)^{1/2k}),\]\nwhere $H_T^i=\epsilon I_{n_i}+\sum_{t=1}^T G_t^{(i)}$ for all $i\in[k]$ and $D=\max_{t\in[T]}\|W_t-W^*\|_F$.
main_theorem.rate: Under standard assumptions each trace term is O(T^{1/2k}), so the product and regret are O(sqrt(T)); the theorem itself gives the explicit comparator-dependent bound.
main_theorem.measure: Online convex regret of Algorithm 2 against a fixed tensor comparator W^*.

key_lemmas.name: Lemma_1_adaptive_OMD_regret
key_lemmas.statement_math: \text{For any sequence of matrices } H_1,\ldots,H_T \succ 0, \text{ the regret of online mirror descent is bounded above by } \frac{1}{2\eta}\sum_{t=1}^T(\|w_t-w^*\|_{H_t}^2-\|w_{t+1}-w^*\|_{H_t}^2)+\frac{\eta}{2}\sum_{t=1}^T(\|g_t\|_{H_t}^*)^2.
key_lemmas.role: Provides the adaptive mirror descent regret inequality used for Theorems 7, 10, and 13.

key_lemmas.name: Lemma_2_FTL_BTL_potential
key_lemmas.statement_math: \text{Let } g_1,\ldots,g_T \text{ be a sequence of vectors, and let } M_t=\sum_{s=1}^t g_sg_s^T \text{ for } t\ge1. \text{ Given a function } \Phi \text{ over PSD matrices, define } H_t=\operatorname*{argmin}_{H\succ0} M_t\bullet H^{-1}+\Phi(H) \text{ (and assume that a minimum is attained for all } t). \text{ Then } \sum_{t=1}^T(\|g_t\|_{H_t}^*)^2 \le \sum_{t=1}^T(\|g_t\|_{H_T}^*)^2+\Phi(H_T)-\Phi(H_0).
key_lemmas.role: Bounds the cumulative adaptive dual norm by the terminal potential in the Shampoo regret proof.

proof.description: Rewrite the desired inequality by moving Phi(H_0) to the left-hand side.
Proceed by induction on T; the base case T=0 is stated to be trivial.
Apply the induction hypothesis up to T-1.
Record the printed FTL objective identity for M_{T-1}; H_{T-1} is a minimizer of this objective.
Use the minimizer property of H_{T-1} in the objective from the previous step to replace H_{T-1} by H_T, giving the second displayed inequality in the induction chain.
proof.ref: Appendix C.1 lines 1290-1293, justified by lines 1295-1301

proof.description: Combine the two inequalities in the displayed induction chain.
Add (||g_T||_{H_T}^*)^2 to both sides to obtain the rewritten target.

key_lemmas.name: Algorithm3_diagonal_preconditioner_monotone
key_lemmas.role: Formalization scaffolding, not a printed source lemma: derives the diagonal-PSD side condition needed when Appendix A applies v^TMv\le\|v\|_\infty^2Tr(M) to M=H_t-H_{t-1}.

proof.description: Record Algorithm 3's initialization and diagonal accumulator recurrences.
proof.math: W_1 = 0_{m \times n};\quad L_0 = \epsilon I_m;\quad R_0 = \epsilon I_n;\quad L_t=L_{t-1}+diag(G_tG_t^T),\quad R_t=R_{t-1}+diag(G_t^TG_t).

proof.description: From the diagonal Gram updates, derive that each increment diag(G_tG_t^T) and diag(G_t^TG_t) is diagonal PSD; hence the accumulated L_t and R_t are diagonal PSD and are monotone in Loewner order. This is a formalization of the side condition behind Appendix A's phrase 'for a diagonal PSD matrix M'.
Apply operator monotonicity of the one-fourth power to the monotone diagonal PSD accumulators, so L_t^{1/4} and R_t^{1/4} are diagonal PSD and remain monotone.

Use the Kronecker PSD/order calculus for the definition H_t=L_t^{1/4}\otimes R_t^{1/4}; since the factors are diagonal PSD and monotone, H_t is diagonal PSD, H_{t-1}\preceq H_t, and H_t-H_{t-1} is diagonal PSD.

key_lemmas.name: Gram_self_product_PSD
key_lemmas.ref: Imported Mathlib PSD fact; source PSD notation Section 2 lines 176-184 and contraction definition lines 631-638
key_lemmas.statement_math: \text{For a real matrix } A,\ AA^T\succeq0 \text{ and } A^TA\succeq0.
key_lemmas.role: Supplies the PSD-increment prerequisite used to derive monotonicity of Shampoo accumulators from the printed recurrences.

key_lemmas.name: Lemma_3_kron_calculus
key_lemmas.statement_math: (i)\ (A\otimes B)(A'\otimes B')=(AA')\otimes(BB');\quad (ii)\ (A\otimes B)^T=A^T\otimes B^T;\quad (iii)\ \text{If } A,B\succeq0, \text{ then } (A\otimes B)^s=A^s\otimes B^s, \text{ and in particular, if } A,B\succ0 \text{ then } (A\otimes B)^{-1}=A^{-1}\otimes B^{-1};\quad (iv)\ \text{If } A\succeq A' \text{ and } B\succeq B' \text{ then } A\otimes B\succeq A'\otimes B', \text{ and in particular, if } A,B\succeq0 \text{ then } A\otimes B\succeq0;\quad (v)\ \operatorname{Tr}(A\otimes B)=\operatorname{Tr}(A)\operatorname{Tr}(B);\quad (vi)\ \operatorname{vec}(uv^T)=u\otimes v.
key_lemmas.role: Supplies Kronecker algebra, trace factorization, PSD order preservation, powers, and rank-one vectorization.

key_lemmas.name: Lemma_4_matrix_kron_vec
key_lemmas.statement_math: \text{Let } G\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n},\ L\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\text{ and } R\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}. \text{ Then } (L\otimes R^T)\operatorname{vec}(G)=\operatorname{vec}(LGR).
key_lemmas.role: Converts Shampoo matrix updates into a single flattened Kronecker-preconditioned gradient step.

proof.description: First prove the identity for rank-one G=uv^T and expand the left hand side using Lemma 3(vi) then Lemma 3(i).
Expand the right hand side for rank-one G=uv^T and use Lemma 3(vi) again.
Extend from rank-one matrices to arbitrary matrices by expressing any matrix as a sum of rank-one matrices and using linearity of all operators involved.

key_lemmas.name: Lemma_5_Ando_geometric_mean
key_lemmas.statement_math: \text{Assume that } 0\preceq X_i\preceq Y_i \text{ for all } i=1,\ldots,n. \text{ Assume further that all } X_i \text{ commute with each other and all } Y_i \text{ commute with each other. Let } \alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n\ge0 \text{ such that } \sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i=1, \text{ then } X_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots X_n^{\alpha_n}\preceq Y_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots Y_n^{\alpha_n}.
key_lemmas.role: Provides operator monotonicity for products of commuting PSD matrices in Lemma 8 and Lemma 11.

key_lemmas.name: Lemma_6_operator_monotone_powers
key_lemmas.statement_math: \text{The function } x\mapsto x^\alpha \text{ is operator-monotone for } \alpha\in[0,1], \text{ that is, if } 0\preceq X\preceq Y \text{ then } X^\alpha\preceq Y^\alpha.
key_lemmas.role: Turns Lemma 8 and Lemma 11 domination into square-root domination of preconditioners.

proof.description: The paper states this as a classic Loewner result and an immediate consequence of Lemma 5.

key_lemmas.name: Theorem_7_matrix_regret
key_lemmas.statement_math: \text{Assume that the gradients } G_1,\ldots,G_T \text{ are matrices of rank at most } r. \text{ Then the regret of Algorithm 1 compared to any } W^*\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} \text{ is bounded as follows, } \sum_{t=1}^T f_t(W_t)-\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(W^*) \le \sqrt{2r}D\operatorname{Tr}(L_T^{1/4})\operatorname{Tr}(R_T^{1/4}), \text{ where } L_T=\epsilon I_m+\sum_{t=1}^TG_tG_t^T,\ R_T=\epsilon I_n+\sum_{t=0}^TG_t^TG_t,\ D=\max_{t\in[T]}\|W_t-W^*\|_F.
key_lemmas.role: Matrix endpoint and proof template for the general tensor theorem.

proof.description: Recall Algorithm 1's matrix update.
Use Lemma 4 to view the left and right preconditioning matrices as the single flattened Kronecker preconditioner H_t=L_t^{1/4}\otimes R_t^{1/4}, with g_t=vec(G_t) and w_t=vec(W_t).
Record Algorithm 1's accumulator initialization and update recurrences before invoking the monotonicity premise in the proof.

This records the strict flattened preconditioner chain required for Lemma 1 while preserving that strict positivity came from the source assertion, not from epsilon >= 0.
Use D=max_t ||w_t-w^*||=max_t ||W_t-W^*||_F and H_0=0 to bound the first Lemma 1 term by the displayed telescoping trace expression.
Combine Lemma 1 with Eq. (3) to obtain the displayed regret inequality Eq. (4).
Use Lemma 8 and operator monotonicity of the square-root function from Lemma 6 to define and bound the hatted full preconditioner.
Choose the potential used in Lemma 2.
Set M_t=\sum_{s=1}^t g_sg_s^T and rewrite the Lemma 2 argmin objective as the displayed trace objective whose minimizer is \widehat H_t.
Justify the displayed minimizer by the paper's derivative calculation for Tr(AX+X^{-1}).
Apply Lemma 2 with the chosen potential and minimizing sequence to get the first inequality in Eq. (6).
Expand the terminal right-hand side using the definition of \widehat H_T and the chosen potential, producing the second inequality printed in Eq. (6).
Use \widehat H_T^2=r\epsilon I+\sum_{t=1}^Tg_tg_t^T to simplify the expanded objective to twice the trace.
Use Eq. (5) once to compare the Algorithm preconditioner dual norm to the hatted dual norm.
Use Eq. (6) to bound the transferred hatted dual-norm sum by 2 sqrt(r) Tr(\widehat H_T).
Use Eq. (5) a second time to replace Tr(\widehat H_T) by sqrt(r) Tr(H_T).
Substitute the dual-norm sum bound into Eq. (4), yielding the coefficient before optimizing eta; this is the left inequality inside the final displayed proof line.
Choose \eta=D/\sqrt{2r} as printed in the proof to simplify the coefficient to \sqrt{2r}D.
Combine the printed eta choice with the Kronecker trace identity for H_T=L_T^{1/4}\otimes R_T^{1/4}; the math field records the final displayed proof line rather than an intermediate equality.

key_lemmas.name: Lemma_8_matrix_rank_domination
key_lemmas.statement_math: \text{Assume that } G_1,\ldots,G_T\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} \text{ are matrices of rank at most } r. \text{ Let } g_t=\operatorname{vec}(G_t) \text{ denote the vectorization of } G_t \text{ for all } t. \text{ Then, for any } \epsilon\ge0,\ \epsilon I_{mn}+\frac{1}{r}\sum_{t=1}^T g_tg_t^T \preceq (\epsilon I_m+\sum_{t=1}^T G_tG_t^T)^{1/2}\otimes(\epsilon I_n+\sum_{t=1}^T G_t^TG_t)^{1/2}.
key_lemmas.role: Main rank-dependent domination that compares the structured matrix preconditioner to a full AdaGrad preconditioner.

proof.description: Introduce the shorthand accumulators A_m and B_n.
proof.math: A_m\stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}\epsilon I_m+\sum_{t=1}^T G_tG_t^T,\quad B_n\stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}\epsilon I_n+\sum_{t=1}^T G_t^TG_t.

proof.description: Use Lemma 9 and the accumulator notation to obtain the two printed upper bounds.
proof.math: \epsilon I_{mn}+\frac1r\sum_{t=1}^T g_tg_t^T\preceq I_m\otimes B_n\quad\text{and}\quad\epsilon I_{mn}+\frac1r\sum_{t=1}^T g_tg_t^T\preceq A_m\otimes I_n.

proof.description: Observe the printed commutativity fact: I_m\otimes B_n and A_m\otimes I_n commute with each other.
Apply Lemma 5 to the commuting upper bounds to get the geometric-mean product bound.
Use Lemma 3(iii) to rewrite the Kronecker powers in the product.
Use Lemma 3(i) to multiply the two Kronecker factors and complete the proof.

key_lemmas.name: Lemma_9_single_matrix_rank_domination
key_lemmas.statement_math: \text{Let } G \text{ be an } m\times n \text{ matrix of rank at most } r \text{ and denote } g=\operatorname{vec}(G). \text{ Then, } \frac{1}{r}gg^T\preceq I_m\otimes(G^TG) \text{ and } \frac{1}{r}gg^T\preceq (GG^T)\otimes I_n.
key_lemmas.role: Single-gradient rank bound used to prove Lemma 8 and, through matricizations, Lemma 11.

proof.description: Write the singular value decomposition and vectorize using Lemma 3(vi).
State the auxiliary vector inequality for any set of vectors w_1,...,w_r.
Introduce the arbitrary quadratic-form test vector x and the scalars alpha_i=x^T w_i that the paper uses to prove the PSD inequality.
proof.produces: Lemma_9_quadratic_test_setup: for arbitrary x, set alpha_i=x^T w_i

proof.description: Apply convexity of alpha -> alpha^2 to the quadratic form, proving the auxiliary vector PSD inequality by testing on x.
Apply the vector inequality to the vectorized SVD expansion and rewrite each term with Lemma 3(i).
Use G G^T = sum sigma_i^2 u_i u_i^T and v_i v_i^T \preceq I_n to get the bound with (GG^T) \otimes I_n.
Similarly use G^T G = sum sigma_i^2 v_i v_i^T and u_i u_i^T \preceq I_m to obtain the other bound.

key_lemmas.name: Lemma_11_tensor_rank_domination
key_lemmas.statement_math: \text{Assume that } G_1,\ldots,G_T \text{ are all order } k \text{ tensors of dimension } n_1\times\cdots\times n_k, \text{ and let } n=n_1\cdots n_k \text{ and } g_t=\operatorname{vec}(G_t) \text{ for all } t. \text{ Let } r_i \text{ denote the bound on the rank of the ith matricization of } G_1,\ldots,G_T, \text{ namely, } \operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{mat}_i(G_t))\le r_i \text{ for all } t \text{ and } i\in[k]. \text{ Denote } r=(\prod_{i=1}^k r_i)^{1/k}. \text{ Then, for any } \epsilon\ge0 \text{ it holds that } \epsilon I_n+\sum_{t=1}^T g_tg_t^T \preceq r\bigotimes_{i=1}^k(\epsilon I_{n_i}+\sum_{t=1}^T G_t^{(i)})^{1/k}.
key_lemmas.role: Tensor analogue of Lemma 8; the key domination input for Theorem 10.

proof.description: For a fixed mode i, apply Lemma 9 to mat_i(G_t), using the rank bound of that matricization.
Use Lemma 15 to translate the matricized-vector inequality into the tensor-vector Kronecker ordering.
Sum over t and add epsilon identity terms, preserving one inequality for each dimension i.
The right-hand side matrices are PSD and commute; apply Lemma 5 with equal weights 1/k and collect the scalar geometric mean of r_i.

key_lemmas.name: Lemma_12_tensor_kron_vec
key_lemmas.statement_math: \text{Let } G \text{ be an } n_1\times\ldots\times n_k \text{ dimensional tensor and } M_i \text{ be an } n_i\times n_i \text{ for } i\in[k], \text{ then } (\bigotimes_{i=1}^k M_i)\operatorname{vec}(G)=\operatorname{vec}(G\times_1M_1\times_2M_2\ldots\times_kM_k).
key_lemmas.role: Shows Algorithm 2's mode-wise tensor preconditioning is a single Kronecker-preconditioned flattened update.

proof.description: Prove by induction on k >= 2; the base case k=2 is Lemma 4.
For the induction step set H to the Kronecker product over the first k-1 modes and rewrite vec(G) as vec(mat_k(G)^T); then apply Lemma 4.
Introduce the k-th-mode slices G_k^1,...,G_k^{n_k}; the paper records that the i-th row of mat_k(G) is vec(G_k^i)^T before invoking induction.
Apply the induction hypothesis to H vec(G_k^i) for each k-th-mode slice.
Stack the n_k vector identities, for i=1,...,n_k, to form n_k by n_{-k} matrices.
Let G' be the partially preconditioned tensor and substitute the stacked identity into the left-hand side already rewritten in step 2.
Transpose the matrix product inside vec, as printed on the next line of the display.
Use the tensor matricization identity B mat_i(A)=mat_i(A x_i B), printed in the margin, with i=k and B=M_k.
Use the printed identity vec(mat_k(G)^T)=vec(G) to remove the final matricization.
Expand the definition of G' to obtain the claimed tensor product identity.

key_lemmas.name: Lemma_14_tensor_vec_mat_identities
key_lemmas.statement_math: \text{For any column vectors } u_1,\ldots,u_k \text{ and order-}k \text{ tensor } A \text{ it holds that: } (i)\ \operatorname{vec}(u_1\circ\cdots\circ u_k)=u_1\otimes\cdots\otimes u_k;\quad (ii)\ \operatorname{mat}_i(u_1\circ\cdots\circ u_k)=u_i(\bigotimes_{i'\ne i}u_{i'})^T;\quad (iii)\ \operatorname{vec}(A)=\operatorname{vec}(\operatorname{mat}_1(A))=\operatorname{vec}(\operatorname{mat}_k(A)^T);\quad (iv)\ \operatorname{mat}_i(A\times_iM)=M\operatorname{mat}_i(A).
key_lemmas.role: Appendix B identity bundle used in Lemmas 11, 12, and 15.

proof.description: Start the induction proof of (i): the statement is trivial for k=1, and the j-th first-dimension slice of the rank-one tensor is u_{1j}(u_2\circ\cdots\circ u_k).
Apply the induction hypothesis to vectorize the slices and obtain the displayed identity for (i).
For (ii), identify the j-th slice along mode i as u_{ij}(u_1\circ\cdots\circ u_{i-1}\circ u_{i+1}\circ\cdots\circ u_k).
Stack the vectorized mode-i slices as rows to obtain the displayed matricization identity (ii).
For (iii), specialize first to a rank-one tensor A=u_1\circ\cdots\circ u_k.
Compute vec(mat_1(A)) in the rank-one case and identify it with vec(A).
Compute vec(mat_k(A)^T) in the rank-one case and identify it with vec(A).
Extend (iii) from rank-one tensors to arbitrary tensors because any tensor can be written as a sum of rank-one tensors and mat_i and vec are linear.
For (iv), start with rank-one A and use the definition of tensor-matrix product to move M onto the i-th factor.
Apply (ii) to the rank-one product to obtain the displayed matrix identity.
Extend (iv) from rank-one tensors to arbitrary A by the linearity of all operators involved.

key_lemmas.name: Lemma_15_matricized_psd_equivalence
key_lemmas.statement_math: \text{Let } G \text{ be an order } k \text{ tensor of dimension } n_1\times\cdots\times n_k, \text{ and } B \text{ an } n_i\times n_i \text{ matrix. Let } g_i=\operatorname{vec}(\operatorname{mat}_i(G)) \text{ and } g=\operatorname{vec}(G). \text{ Then } g_ig_i^T\preceq B\otimes\bigotimes_{j\ne i}I_{n_j}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ gg^T\preceq\left(\bigotimes_{j<i}I_{n_j}\right)\otimes B\otimes\left(\bigotimes_{j>i}I_{n_j}\right).
key_lemmas.role: Transfers Lemma 9's matricized PSD inequality back to the tensor vectorization order in Lemma 11.

proof.description: Test the two PSD inequalities on an arbitrary tensor X and define x and x_i.
proof.math: x=\operatorname{vec}(X),\quad x_i=\operatorname{vec}(\operatorname{mat}_i(X));\quad x_i^Tg_ig_i^Tx_i\le x_i^T(B\otimes\bigotimes_{j\ne i}I_{n_j})x_i \Longleftrightarrow x^Tgg^Tx\le x^T((\bigotimes_{j<i}I_{n_j})\otimes B\otimes(\bigotimes_{j>i}I_{n_j}))x.

proof.description: Note that the two left-hand sides are equal because both are the squared dot product of tensors G and X.
Write X in the standard tensor basis, with alpha ranging over all k-tuples and e_{alpha_j} the standard unit vectors.
Vectorize the tensor-basis expansion of X in the order used by vec.
Insert the vectorized basis expansion into the tensor-order quadratic form.
Apply the identity matrices and B to the basis vector in the tensor-order quadratic form.
Expand the remaining x^T using the same basis vectorization, yielding the double sum over alpha and alpha'.
Use the orthogonality of the standard basis vectors, as stated in the text after the display, to reduce the double sum to the final tensor-order RHS.
Recall the paper's displayed expansion of mat_i(X).
Vectorize the displayed expansion of mat_i(X).
Insert the vectorized matricization expansion into the matricized-order quadratic form.
Apply B and the identity matrices to the basis vector in the matricized-order quadratic form.
Expand x_i^T, then use the same standard-basis orthogonality to reach the matching final sum.
Conclude the right-hand sides are equal, and together with left-hand side equality this proves the equivalence.

key_lemmas.name: Theorem_13_diagonal_matrix_regret
key_lemmas.statement_math:
Theorem 13. Assume that the gradients $G_1,\ldots,G_T$ are matrices of rank at most $r$. Then the regret of Algorithm 3 compared to any $W^*\in\mathbb{R}^{m	imes n}$ is bounded as
\[\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(W_t)-\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(W^*)\le \sqrt{2r}D_\infty Tr(L_T^{1/4})Tr(R_T^{1/4}),\]
where
\[L_T=\epsilon I_m+\sum_{t=1}^T diag(G_tG_t^T),\quad R_T=\epsilon I_n+\sum_{t=0}^T diag(G_t^TG_t),\quad D_\infty=\max_{t\in[T]}\|W_t-W^*\|_\infty.\]
(Here, $\|A\|_\infty$ is the entry-wise $\ell_\infty$ norm of a matrix $A$, i.e., $\|A\|_\infty\stackrel{def}{=}\|vec(A)\|_\infty$.)

source_discrepancies.name: Appendix_A_diagonal_monotonicity_scaffolding_not_printed
source_discrepancies.description: Appendix A defines H_t=L_t^{1/4}\otimes R_t^{1/4} and applies the inequality v^TMv<=||v||_infty^2 Tr(M) for a diagonal PSD matrix M, but it does not print a standalone lemma saying L_t, R_t, their one-fourth powers, H_t, and H_t-H_{t-1} are diagonal PSD or monotone. Algorithm3_diagonal_preconditioner_monotone is therefore marked as formalization scaffolding whose source math is limited to the printed H_t definition and whose derived PSD/order facts are recorded in proof produces fields.

source_discrepancies.name: Epsilon_PD_condition_not_explicit_in_theorem_heads
source_discrepancies.ref: Algorithms 1-3; Proof of Theorem 7 lines 489-490; Lemmas 8 and 11
source_discrepancies.description: Algorithms initialize with epsilon times the identity and Lemmas 8/11 state epsilon >= 0, but Lemma 1 requires H_1,...,H_T > 0 and the proof of Theorem 7 asserts 0 < H_1 <= ... <= H_T via 0 < L_1 <= ... <= L_T and 0 < R_1 <= ... <= R_T. With epsilon=0 and zero or rank-deficient early gradients, Algorithm 1/2 recurrences plus Gram PSD increments prove only non-strict PSD monotonicity, not the strict-positive premise. The Theorem_7_matrix_regret, Theorem_10_tensor_regret, and Theorem_13_diagonal_matrix_regret proof traces therefore mark the strict chain as source-asserted/formalization-side-condition rather than derived from Epsilon_nonnegative_rank_lemmas or the diagonal PSD monotonicity scaffolding.
